The long read · Housing

The eighties are back for homebuyers. This time it is the price, not the rate.

In 1981 the thirty-year mortgage rate averaged 16.64%, the highest of the years shown, on a median home of about $66,400. By 2025 the rate was 6.60% and the home cost about $407,000. Add up what each buyer pays over ten years and the two land in the same place.

In 2025 the thirty-year rate averaged 6.60% and the median existing home cost about $407,000, 4.65 years of household income. The comparison needs a second year in view.

One number for a decade of owning

A month's payment tells only part of it. The fair test of whether a home was affordable is everything a buyer paid to own it: the cash to close, then ten years of payments, with property tax, insurance and any refinance along the way, set against everything the household earned in those same ten years.

On that test the buyer from 2025 comes to 38.7% of ten years' income. The hardest of the buyers whose ten years are all on record, from 1981, came to 39.1%; the easiest, from 2012, 24.9%; no buyer in view has all ten years on record yet.

On that test the 2025 buyer comes to 38.7% of ten years' income.

How close is close? Across every year bought, today's buyer lands within about a point of the worst, with no refinance. One refinance a point lower would put them well below it. The eighties prices are NAR's own figures; today's is pinned to NAR's latest months; the years between are an estimate. Read the two as close, not as a ranking.

Then it was the rate. Now it is the price.What the year in view asked of a buyer

The same burden can come from two places. In the early eighties homes were cheap against incomes, and money was dear; today money is merely ordinary, and homes are dear. The cards set the highest-rate year beside the latest, on the three tests a buyer meets, and mark the harder of each pair.

The eighties buyer got a way out. Today's has not, yet.

A high rate is a burden you can refinance; a high price is not. Follow three buyers through the years after they bought, each panel on the same scale. The early-eighties buyer's payment shrank as rates fell and they refinanced, and as their income grew. The latest buyers' lines stop where the data does.

Forty-odd years in three lines

Decade by decade

The twenty-tens were the easy decade, and the nineties the next easiest: rates fell under buyers who already owned, and prices held near three and a half years of income. The two hard stretches, the early eighties and now, are hard for opposite reasons, which is why the policy each needs is opposite too.

Click a decade to read the whole page for it, or pick one above.

Your turn: change the projection

A what-if on your own inputs: it changes no figure on the page and is not part of the trace. It starts from the same assumption as the chart: rates stay put, and income and home values keep growing at income's pace over the last decade. The rate a refinance could reach matters most; leave it at today's rate for no refinance.

Sources

  • Mortgage rate. Freddie Mac, Primary Mortgage Market Survey: thirty-year fixed, weekly, averaged to each year.
  • Existing-home price. The National Association of Realtors' median existing-home price. Through the early twenty-tens, NAR's own annual figures, as HUD reprinted them in U.S. Housing Market Conditions (and a later edition). NAR does not publish its annual history freely after that, so later years are an estimate: the FHFA repeat-sales house price index, pinned to NAR at both ends — its last reprinted year and its latest months.
  • New-home price, for contrast. U.S. Census Bureau and HUD, median sales price of houses sold, mostly new construction.
  • Household income. U.S. Census Bureau, median household income (CPS ASEC, table H-5), current dollars.
  • One earner's pay. BLS, median usual weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers, times fifty-two.

What this leaves out

  • Where you live. These are national medians. In the most expensive metros prices run far higher against local incomes, and this report has no metro series to compare eras there.
  • Local taxes and insurance. Both are one national rate for every year, so no era gets a friendlier assumption. Real bills vary a lot by place; set yours in the what-if.
  • Refinancing costs are left out, which slightly flatters buyers who refinanced, the eighties buyer included. Mortgage insurance on a smaller down payment is left out too.
  • The future. Any buyer whose ten years run past the data gets projected years, on one stated assumption, and is marked projected everywhere. The projection is a what-if, not a forecast.
Down payment 20% assumed for every buyer · typed, not a query
Closing costs 3% of the price · typed, not a query
Property tax and insurance 1.45% of the home's value a year · typed, not a query
The method, in words

Each year's buyer puts a fifth down on the median existing home, pays closing costs, and takes a thirty-year fixed loan at that year's average rate. The monthly payment adds property tax and insurance, at the same national rates every year. Buyers are then followed for up to a decade: they refinance when rates fall a full point, their taxes grow with the home's value, and each year's payment is measured against that year's median income. Years past the data are projected: the rate stays at the latest year's average, and income and home values grow at income's pace over the last decade. The work is in transforms/affordability_transform.py; refresh the data from the publishers with python inputs/fetch_housing.py before citing a figure (inputs/housing_sources.md).

Built Oct 30, 2026 · Housing Affordability. This page does not claim the numbers are right.

How these numbers were made

This file carries its trace: each figure names the query that produced it and a fingerprint of the result. tracebi verify re-runs those queries and checks whether the numbers still match the model.

the transform 'affordability' states: one row per year from inputs/housing_history.csv: Freddie Mac 30-year average rate; existing-home price = NAR's annual median through 2012 (as reprinted by HUD), then the FHFA repeat-sales index pinned to NAR at both ends; Census/HUD median price of houses sold (mostly new) for contrast; Census median household income; BLS median full-time weekly earnings x 52. Payment = principal and interest (20% down, 30 years, that year's rate) + property tax 1.1% + insurance 0.35% of value a year. Entry cost = 20% down + 3% closing. Cohort paths refinance at a one-point drop, for up to ten years. Ten-year shares past the last year are projected: rate held at the last year's average, income and home values growing at income's last-decade pace.

· rows(fact_housing): the series starts in 1979; fewer rows means a truncated pull

measure 'years_in_view': Years in view: fact_housing has one row per year

measure 'mortgage_rate': 30-year fixed rate, annual average, in percent

measure 'price_to_income': Existing-home price as a multiple of median household income

measure 'existing_price': Median existing-home price (FHFA repeat-sales index scaled to NAR's median)

measure 'median_income': Median household income

measure 'entry_cost': Cash to close: 20% down plus 3% closing costs

measure 'payment': Monthly principal, interest, property tax and insurance on the median existing home, 20% down

measure 'entry_share': Cash to close as a share of a year's median household income

measure 'payment_share': A year of full payments as a share of median household income

measure 'earner_share': A year of full payments as a share of one full-time earner's pay

measure 'rate_held': The rate the buyer holds that year, after any refinance

measure 'housing_share': Cash to close plus every payment, as a share of the household income earned over the same years

measure 'years_measured': How many of a buyer's ten years are in the data; the rest are projected

measure 'rate_at_purchase': Rate at purchase

measure 'price_at_purchase': Existing-home price at purchase

measure 'income_at_purchase': Median household income at purchase

measure 'assumed_rate': Rate assumed for projected years: the last year's average

measure 'growth_pct': Yearly income and home-value growth assumed for projected years: income's last-decade pace, in percent

measure 'price_growth': Median existing-home price, change on the year before

measure 'income_growth': Median household income, change on the year before
